## Household and background

Susan Miranda (born January 26, 1984 — 41 all through the tax year, so no age-55 HSA catch-up) is single with no dependents, renting an apartment at 58 Corliss Avenue in Anytown. She has worked all year as an office manager at Brightwell Office Systems Inc — one W-2, box 1 wages $39,674.00, box 2 federal withholding $7,274.00.

The tax story this year is her health coverage. Through June 30 she was enrolled in her employer's self-only high-deductible health plan (HDHP) with a linked HSA. On July 1 the company switched everyone to a low-deductible PPO that is not HSA-eligible, so her HDHP coverage ran exactly six months (January-June). Her employer seeded $260.00 into the HSA during the spring (W-2 box 12, code W), and she made small payroll contributions of her own: $690.00 during 2025, plus another $80.00 in February 2026 that she asked the custodian to count toward 2025. She did not spend anything out of the HSA this year.

## Interview

**Q.** Which months of 2025 were you covered by the high-deductible plan?

**A.** January through June — the company changed plans on July 1.

**Q.** On December 1, 2025, were you covered by an HDHP?

**A.** No. The replacement PPO is not a high-deductible plan, so my HDHP coverage ended June 30.

**Q.** Was the HDHP self-only or family coverage?

**A.** Self-only — it's just me.

**Q.** Besides the $260 your employer put in, did you contribute to the HSA yourself?

**A.** Yes — $690 through payroll during the year, and $80 more in February 2026 that I told the custodian to apply to 2025.

**Q.** Did you take any money out of the HSA in 2025?

**A.** No — I'm leaving it to grow and saving my receipts.

**Q.** Were you enrolled in Medicare, covered under anyone else's health plan, or claimable as a dependent on someone else's return?

**A.** No to all three.

- Line 11 room = $2,150 − $260 employer contribution = $1,890; HSA deduction (line 13) = min($770 own contributions, $1,890) = $770 → Schedule 1 line 13.
